summary: Murrieta sits in a broad inland valley between the Santa Rosa Plateau to the west and the foothills of the San Jacinto range to the east, which means winter sunsets light up a genuine ridgeline rather than disappearing behind rooftops — an unusual perk for a city that grew almost entirely after 1990 and is laid out in the master-planned, wide-arterial style that implies otherwise. At 35 square miles and just over 111,000 residents, it delivers a density of roughly 3,100 people per square mile — suburban enough that most errands involve a car, but filled enough that retail centers, medical offices, and chain restaurants cluster at regular intervals along Interstate 15 and Murrieta Hot Springs Road. The economy leans heavily on healthcare (Loma Linda University Medical Center–Murrieta is a major anchor) and public-sector employment, though a large share of earners commute north toward Temecula, Riverside, or even San Diego County, making I-15 congestion a defining daily friction. A median household income near $110,000 against a median home price around $607,000 yields a price-to-income ratio just under 5.5× — tight but within conventional lending reach, a contrast to coastal Southern California where that ratio often exceeds 8×. With nearly 10 hours of daily sunshine on average and daytime highs that hover in the mid-70s annually, outdoor time is year-round, and the Santa Rosa Plateau Ecological Reserve — a legitimate open-space preserve with vernal pools and grassland trails — sits minutes from the city's western edge. Murrieta is, at its core, a place engineered for commuters who traded coastal proximity for square footage and sunshine, and that bargain defines almost every daily tradeoff here.
